title: me- verbs
pattern: me- + root + what it's done to: membeli tiket · in speech: beli tiket
explanation: me- makes a verb where someone does something to something: membeli tiket (to buy a ticket), membaca buku (to read a book), memesan kamar (to book a room). It also turns some nouns into verbs: rokok is a cigarette, merokok is to smoke. Writing, signs, the news and careful speech keep the me-, which is a big part of why written Indonesian looks longer than what you hear. In conversation it usually drops (Saya beli tiket kemarin, Cari apa?), and friends often use a form starting with ng- or ny- instead: ngambil for mengambil, nyari for mencari, nonton for menonton.
natural: Keep me- in anything written (a message to a hotel, an email, a form) and when you want to sound careful, for example with an official. With shop staff, drivers and neighbours, the bare root is polite enough: Saya mau beli dua.
stiff: A short spoken sentence full of me- sounds read aloud: at a ticket window, Saya ingin membeli dua tiket is correct but bookish, and Beli dua tiket, ya is what people say. The ng- and ny- forms are casual, so keep them for friends.

gap.note: Beli is just as right, and it's what most people say out loud; membeli is the written and careful form.
gap.why: Saya does the buying to the tickets, so it's the me- verb: membeli.

examples.english: I'll just grab a coffee first.

gap.why: Talking to a friend, the me- drops and the root does the job: beli; dibeli is passive, and pembeli is a buyer.

examples.indonesian: Saya belum memutuskan mau ke mana.
examples.english: I haven't decided where to go yet.

gap.why: Deciding is memutuskan; putus on its own means broken off or split up, so this me- stays even in speech.
Smoking is me- + rokok (a cigarette); perokok is a smoker.
